text: Marcel-André Baschet (5 August 1862 – 28 December 1941) was a French portrait painter renowned for his many portraits of the Presidents of the French Third Republic. Born in Gagny (Seine-et-Oise), he was the second son of Ludovic Baschet, who was the art editor of Panorama and the Revue illustrée. His brother René served as art critic for Salonsavant and edited L'Illustration from 1904 until the first half of the 20th century. At age 17, Baschet enrolled at the Académie Julian in the studio of Jules Lefebvre. He studied at the École des beaux-arts de Paris under Gustave Boulanger, and in 1883 won the Grand Prix de Rome for his painting Oedipus curses his son Polynices, becoming a pensionist at the Villa Médicis in Rome from 1883 to 1887. On 3 January 1888, he married Jeanne Guillemeteau, with whom he had one son and one daughter. He began teaching at the Académie Julian in 1889 and from 1900 taught Princess Mathilde. From 1907 to 1941, he operated a shop at 21 Quai Voltaire in Paris, where a commemorative plaque was installed after his death. In 1908, he received the médaille d'honneur for his portrait of Henri Rochefort, and his portrait of Claude Debussy was exhibited globally. He was awarded the Knight of the Légion d'honneur in 1898 and was elected a member of the Académie des beaux-arts in 1913. His artworks are held in private collections and museums, including the Musée d'Orsay and Château de Versailles. His younger brother Jacques (1872–1952) was a historian, art critic, artistic director, and editor of L'Illustration, as well as director of a national company.
